thread.title: Apple's Services segment is on a growth tear (AAPL)

author: Audrey Schomer (aschomer@businessinsider.com)
title: Apple's Services segment is on a growth tear (AAPL)
text:
Audrey Schomer 3m This story was delivered to Business Insider Intelligence " Digital Media Briefing " subscribers hours before appearing on Business Insider. To be the first to know, please click here .
On its path to being the first company ever to reach a $1 trillion market cap, Apple continued to fuel revenue growth with its Services segment this quarter, which reached an all-time high of $9.5 billion, according to its Q2 earnings results released on Tuesday.
Business Insider Intelligence
Services — which includes the App Store, ApplePay, iCloud, and Apple Music — now makes up 18% of overall quarterly revenue at the tech company, up from 16% in Q2 2017.
Overall company revenues hit $53.3 billion, up 17% year-over-year (YoY), the company's fourth straight quarter of double-digit growth.
What makes Services so valuable is that apps in this segment can be distributed to an active installed base of roughly 1.3 billion devices.
As Apple seeks revenue diversification beyond iPhone sales, Services effectively monetizes those sales further. Apple CEO Tim Cook's comments on the call hinted at expansion plans that would further scale Services.
Growth in the Services unit is being driven in part by Apple's subscriptions business. Nearly 30,000 third-party apps sell subscriptions through the App Store. And in the past year, Apple has sold more than 300 million subscriptions through both its own apps (like Apple Music) and third-party apps (like publishers' apps), up more than 60% YoY.
Apple doesn't break out revenues that derive from these subscriptions, but they're likely significant, and Cook said subscriptions are contributing a rising percentage of Services' revenues. Apple takes a percentage share of monthly fees for any subscriptions sold through the App Store — it takes a 30% cut in the first year, and 15% every year thereafter. For example, the $9.99-a-month music-streaming service Apple Music now has well over 50 million subs — up from the roughly 40 million it had in April — with revenues up 50% YoY.
The subscriptions business could also ramp up as soon as we learn more about Apple's content plans.Apple is reportedly planning to upgrade the Apple News app with a premium news subscription service that would essentially bundle magazine offerings for a monthly fee.
The tech company has also been investing in premium original video content, including a deal with Oprah. Although it's unclear how Apple plans to distribute its video content, it's likely to become either part of another subscription offering like Apple Music, or part of a new catch-all one, such as a double- or triple-play bundle that integrates Apple News, Apple Music, and "Apple Video."
In any case, Cook is bearish on the future of legacy distribution, saying he thinks cord-cutting will accelerate at a "much faster rate than is widely thought." Cord-cutting is expected to rise 33% this year to 33 million adults, up from roughly 25 million cord-cutters at year-end 2017, per eMarketer. Generally thought to be late in the game — coming into original content production long after Netflix — Apple could actually be right on time.
